Existing from 57 BCE to 935 CE and forming the Three Kingdoms of Korea alongside Paekche and Goguryeo, which kingdom had the smallest population of the three?
Silla: Korean kingdom (57 BCE–935 CE). Silla was one of the longest-lasting countries in Korean history.
Writing under the pseudonym 'Frank Talk,' this South African activist led the grassroots Black Consciousness Movement against apartheid in the late 1960s and 1970s — who is he?
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley
Steve Biko: South African anti-apartheid activist (1946–1977)
Described in its founding text as formless, eternal, and the 'Mother of the universe,' this East Asian philosophical concept's Chinese character means 'the way' or 'path' — what is it?
Tao: Philosophical concept native to China.

Named as a single people by the ancient Greeks, this Indo-European group inhabited modern Bulgaria, Romania, and parts of Greece and Turkey, giving rise to tribes like the Getae and Dacians — who were they?
Thracians: Indo-European people in ancient southeast Europe.
Leading Sweden's Moderate Party since 2017, this politician became prime minister in 2022 at the head of a minority coalition and went on to complete his country's accession to NATO. Who is he?
Ulf Kristersson: Prime Minister of Sweden since 2022. Kristersson became party leader after Anna Kinberg Batra resigned in 2017.
A former central bank governor who tamed hyperinflation, he became Ukraine's third president in 2005 on a platform of turning the country toward the EU and NATO. Who is he?
Viktor Yushchenko: President of Ukraine from 2005 to 2010.
Best known for playing 'Trapper' John McIntyre on the CBS series M*A*S*H, this actor later became a regular panelist on a Fox News investing show — who is he?
Hieronymus Karl Friedrich, Freiherr von Münchhausen
Fought between 1939 and 1945, this global conflict remains history's deadliest, claiming 60 to 75 million lives and ending with the only nuclear weapons ever used in war — which conflict?
World War II: 1939–1945 global conflict. World War II, or the Second World War (1 September 1939 – 2 September 1945), was a global conflict between two coalitions: the Allies and the Axis powers.

Regarded as the fourth person to accept Islam, this former slave became the adopted son of the Prophet Muhammad and later commanded early Muslim military expeditions, including a final raid on Byzantine-held Bosra in 629 CE — who was he?
Zayd ibn Haritha al-Kalbi: Companion and adopted son of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four. After helping found Shu Han, Zhuge Liang exercised near-total authority over both civil and military affairs.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Qian Xuesen (born 1911) is the earliest of the four. Qian received his undergraduate education in mechanical engineering at National Chiao Tung University in Shanghai in 1934.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
Earth (formed ~4.54 billion years ago) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
John Archibald Wheeler is a physicist. John Archibald Wheeler (July 9, 1911 – April 13, 2008) was an American theoretical physicist.
Which of these is a mathematician?
Joseph Liouville is a mathematician. The crater Liouville on the Moon is named after him.
What is the atomic number of Bohrium?
Bohrium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Bh and atomic number 107.
What is the atomic number of Platinum?
Platinum is a chemical element; it has symbol Pt and atomic number 78.
In what year was Kalpana Chawla born?
Kalpana Chawla (July 1, 1962 – February 1, 2003) was an Indian-American astronaut and aerospace engineer who was the first woman of Indian origin to fly to space.
In what year was Peter Piot born?
Peter Piot: Sir Peter Karel, Baron Piot (born 17 February 1949) is a Belgian-British microbiologist known for his research into Ebola and AIDS.
In what year was Ibn Khaldun born?
Ibn Khaldun (27 May 1332 – 17 March 1406, 732–808 AH) was an Arab scholar, historian, philosopher, and sociologist.
In what year did H. H. Holmes die?
H. H. Holmes: Holmes, was an American con artist and serial killer active between 1891 and 1894.
In what year did Dmitri Mendeleev die?
Dmitri Mendeleev: The synthetic element mendelevium is named in his honor.
In what year was Magnesium discovered?
Magnesium is a chemical element; it has symbol Mg and atomic number 12.
Adenosine: Pfizer. Adenosine (symbol A) is an organic compound that occurs widely in nature in the form of diverse derivatives.
In which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17 based?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17: Soviet Union. The MiG-17 was license-built in China as the Shenyang J-5 and Poland as the PZL-Mielec Lim-6.
Who is credited with discovering Niobium?
Niobium: Charles Hatchett. Niobium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nb (formerly columbium, Cb) and atomic number 41.
Who is credited with discovering Peroxisome?
Peroxisome: Christian de Duve. A peroxisome is a membrane-bound organelle, a type of microbody, found in the cytoplasm of virtually all eukaryotic cells.
Who is credited with discovering Uncertainty principle?
Uncertainty principle: Werner Heisenberg. The uncertainty principle, also known as Heisenberg's indeterminacy principle, is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics.
Who is credited with discovering Mensa?
Mensa (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is Latin for table, though it originally commemorated Table Mountain and was known as "Mons Mensae".

Belonging to the birch family and numbering about 35 species, these monoecious trees and shrubs are found across the north temperate zone, with a few extending into Central America and the Andes — name this genus of tree?
Alder are trees of the genus Alnus in the birch family Betulaceae.

Usually a symptom of coronary artery disease caused by atherosclerosis narrowing the arteries, this chest pain or pressure gets its name from Latin words meaning 'to strangle' and 'chest' — name this condition?
Angina is chest pain or pressure, usually caused by insufficient blood flow to the heart muscle (myocardium).
Sharing chemistry with phosphorus and antimony, this group-15 metalloid carries the symbol As and a notorious reputation for toxicity — what is it?
Arsenic is a chemical element; it has the symbol As and atomic number 33.
The second-largest living rodents after capybaras, these large semiaquatic mammals of the Northern Hemisphere have webbed back feet, hand-like front paws, and flat, scaly tails — name the animal?
Beaver (genus Castor) are large semiaquatic rodents of the Northern Hemisphere.
In this distributed ledger, each record carries a cryptographic hash of the one before it, so altering any block would mean rewriting every block that follows — what is this technology called?
Blockchain is a distributed ledger with growing lists of records (blocks) that are securely linked together via cryptographic hashes.
This English guard-dog breed combines the size of the Mastiff with genes from the extinct Old English Bulldog, and gained Kennel Club recognition in 1924 — which breed?
Bullmastiff is an English breed of dog of mastiff type and large size, with a solid build and a short muzzle.
This Mexican business magnate was ranked the richest person in the world by Forbes from 2010 to 2013, building his fortune through a sprawling conglomerate called Grupo Carso. Who is he?
Carlos Slim (born 28 January 1940) is a Mexican business oligarch, investor and philanthropist.

Sold under the brand name Thorazine, this phenothiazine antipsychotic treats schizophrenia and bipolar disorder — but it's also been used for nausea, pre-surgery anxiety, and even stubborn hiccups. What is it?
Chlorpromazine (CPZ), marketed under the brand names Thorazine and Largactil among others, is an antipsychotic medication.

This highly venomous, nocturnal snake, black or bluish-black with narrow white crossbands, is widely distributed across South Asia, from grasslands to agricultural fields to human settlements — what snake is it?
Common krait (Bungarus caeruleus) is a highly venomous snake species belonging to the genus Bungarus in the family Elapidae.

Named for a mythological Greek youth who was transformed into a tree after accidentally killing a beloved stag, this genus of evergreen conifers is considered polyphyletic by modern genetic analysis — what genus is it?
Cupressus (common name cypress) is one of several genera of evergreen conifers within the family Cupressaceae; for the others, see cypress.
Caused by a Corynebacterium bacterium, this infection can spin a tough grey 'pseudomembrane' across the throat that slowly chokes off the airway — what is it?
Diphtheria is an infection caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium diphtheriae. The pseudomembrane can grow to cover a wide area of the throat, leading to strangulation and death.
A onetime clerk for Justice Thurgood Marshall, this Harvard Law School dean was tapped for the Supreme Court by President Obama in 2010 — who is she?
Elena Kagan (born April 28, 1960) is an American lawyer who serves as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States.
They're a tiny minority by headcount among living things, yet their larger bodies make their combined biomass dwarf that of bacteria and archaea — what membrane-bound-nucleus group is this?
Eukaryote are the domain Eukaryota or Eukarya, organisms whose cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.
This omnivorous insect, common in North American homes, gets its name from ear-shaped hindwings and carries pincers on its abdomen — which species?
Forficula auricularia is a species complex comprising the common earwig.
Among the longest of all living crocodilians, this fish-eater has a slender snout lined with 110 interlocking teeth and a pot-shaped bulb on the males' noses — what is it?
Gharial (Gavialis gangeticus), also known as gavial or fish-eating crocodile, is a crocodilian in the family Gavialidae and among the longest of all living crocodilians.
Born Herman Webster Mudgett, this con artist and killer worked his crimes around the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, earning the nickname "the Beast of Chicago" — who was he?
H. H. Holmes (May 16, 1861 - May 7, 1896), better known as Dr.

Often called the "father of the Indian nuclear programme," this theoretical physicist founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and the research centre later renamed in his honour. Who was he?
Homi J. Bhabha (30 October 1909 - 24 January 1966) was an Indian nuclear theoretical physicist who is widely credited as the "father of the Indian nuclear programme".

Forming at or below zero degrees Celsius, this naturally occurring crystalline solid is technically classified as a mineral and appears on Earth, other planets, and even in interstellar space — what is it?
Ice is water that is frozen into a solid state, typically forming at or below temperatures of 0 C, 32 F, or 273.15 K.
This Brussels chemist ran a famous five-year willow tree experiment and coined the word 'gas' from the Greek for chaos — who was he?
Jan Baptist van Helmont (12 January 1580 - 30 December 1644) was a chemist, physiologist, and physician from Brussels.
Linked to a herpesvirus and immune suppression, this cancer causing purple skin lesions was already being described by Hippocrates in the 300s BC — which condition?
Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a type of cancer that can form masses on the skin, in lymph nodes, in the mouth, or in other organs.
This small Arctic rodent is a key prey source for tundra carnivores and is the subject of a persistent myth that it marches off cliffs in mass suicide — what animal is it?
Lemming is a small rodent, usually found in or near the Arctic in tundra biomes.
This evergreen tree, native to the cooler hills of south-central China, is grown commercially for its orange fruit and is sometimes called the Japanese medlar. What is it?
Loquat (Eriobotrya japonica) is a large evergreen shrub or tree grown commercially for its orange coloured fruits.
Following fieldwork with the Omaha people and in Papua New Guinea and Bali, this anthropologist explored gender roles in her 1935 book Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies — who is she?
Margaret Mead (December 16, 1901 - November 15, 1978) was an American cultural anthropologist, author and speaker, who appeared frequently in the mass media during the mid-twentieth century.
This British-Lebanese geometer co-founded topological K-theory and lent his name to a famous index theorem — and won both the Fields Medal and the Abel Prize. Who was he?
Michael Atiyah (22 April 1929 - 11 January 2019) was a British-Lebanese mathematician specialising in geometry.
This Turkish government minister for environment and climate will preside over the 2026 UN Climate Change Conference, COP31 — who is he?
Murat Kurum is the minister of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change in Turkey, and president of the 2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31.

A former director of Russia's FSB intelligence agency, this politician served as Secretary of the Security Council of Russia from 2008 to 2024 and is considered one of Putin's closest advisors — who is he?
Nikolai Patrushev (born 11 July 1951) is a Russian politician, security officer and former intelligence officer who served as the secretary of the Security Council of Russia from 2008 to 2024.
Listed by Ptolemy and named for a hunter in Greek myth, this winter constellation boasts the supergiant stars Rigel and Betelgeuse and a famous short, straight line of three stars — which is it?
Orion (constellation) is a prominent set of stars visible during winter in the northern celestial hemisphere.
Known in the US as a goober and in the UK as a monkey nut, this Fabaceae crop hides its edible seeds in underground pods. What is it?

Peanut (Arachis hypogaea), also known as the groundnut, goober (US, via Kikongo), goober pea, pindar (US, via Kikongo) or monkey nut (UK), is a legume crop grown mainly for its edible seeds, contained in underground pods.
Whether captured electronically on a sensor or chemically on light-sensitive film, this art and practice of recording light also powers science and manufacturing — think photolithography. What is it?

Photography is the art, application, and practice of creating images by recording light, either electronically by means of an image sensor, or chemically by means of a light-sensitive material such as photographic film.
Part of the critical theory framework and closely tied to critical race theory, this field analyzes history, literature, and discourse shaped by imperial power — what field is it?

Postcolonialism is the academic study of the cultural, political and economic consequences of colonialism and imperialism, focusing on the impact of human control and exploitation of colonized people and their lands.

Picture benzene, but with one CH swapped for a nitrogen: this flammable, weakly alkaline liquid reeks of fish and underpins countless drugs and vitamins, churned out at 20,000 tons a year — what compound is it?
Pyridine is a basic heterocyclic organic compound with the chemical formula C5H5N.
Also known as vitamin B2, this nutrient builds two key coenzymes for energy metabolism and may, taken orally, cut down on migraine headaches in adults — what is it?
Riboflavin is a vitamin found in food and sold as a dietary supplement.

This volatile, colorless, and odorless nerve agent is so potent a chemical weapon that inhaling a lethal dose can cause death from respiratory paralysis within one to ten minutes — what's the compound called?
Sarin (NATO designation GB short for G-series, B) is an extremely toxic organophosphorus compound that has been often used as a chemical weapon due to its extreme potency as a nerve agent.
Despite its long-nosed, mouse-like look, this small mammal is actually a closer cousin to hedgehogs and moles than to rodents — what is it?
Shrew (family Soricidae) are small mole-like mammals classified in the order Eulipotyphla.

This class of moisture-loving hexapods — the largest lineage of six-legged creatures excluded from the insect group — indirectly aids decomposition by breaking down organic matter and shaping soil microbial life. What are they?
Springtail (class Collembola) form the largest of the three lineages of modern hexapods that are no longer considered insects, the others being Protura and Diplura.

This genus of about a dozen woody flowering shrubs in the olive family, native from southeastern Europe to East Asia, is closely related to privet and provides food for several moth larvae — what is it commonly called?
Syringa is a genus of 12 currently recognized species of flowering woody plants in the olive family called lilacs.
This condition causes abnormally low platelet levels in the blood, leading to prolonged or excessive bleeding — what blood disorder is it?
Thrombocytopenia is a condition characterized by abnormally low levels of platelets (also known as thrombocytes) in the blood.
These large, heavyset American game birds have a distinctive fleshy growth called a snood hanging from the base of their beak, with wild and ocellated species. What birds are they?
Turkey (bird) are large, heavyset galliforms in the genus Meleagris, indigenous to the Americas.
An American investor and philanthropist, he is the chairman of Berkshire Hathaway and, as of January 2026, the ninth-richest person in the world. Who is he?
Warren Buffett (born August 30, 1930) is an American investor and philanthropist who is the chairman and former CEO of the conglomerate Berkshire Hathaway.
Also known as AZT, this was the very first antiretroviral drug used against HIV/AIDS, and can be given during birth to prevent mother-to-child spread — what is it?
Zidovudine (ZDV), also known as azidothymidine (AZT), was the first antiretroviral medication used to prevent and treat HIV/AIDS.
Nicknamed the cell's "molecular unit of currency," this energy-carrying molecule powers muscle contraction and nerve impulses, dropping to ADP or AMP when spent — what is it?
Adenosine triphosphate: Energy-carrying molecule in living cells.
This French surgeon won a 1912 Nobel for pioneering blood-vessel suturing and later teamed with aviator Charles Lindbergh to build an early perfusion pump for organ work. Who was he?
Alexis Carrel: French surgeon and biologist (1873–1944)
Domesticated in Southwest China roughly 2,000 years ago, this corm-producing plant is nicknamed 'devil's tongue' and gets boiled down into a jelly-like noodle called shirataki — what is it?
Amorphophallus konjac: Edible plant from Yunnan, China.
This self-taught Dutch draper turned lensmaker began exploring microbial life with his own single-lensed microscopes in the 1670s, earning him the title 'Father of Microbiology' — who was he?
This American psychiatrist and pharmaceutical marketer amassed the world's largest personal collection of Chinese art, later donated to the Smithsonian — who is he?
Arthur M. Sackler: American physician and executive (1913–1987)
Sold under the brand name Lioresal, this muscle relaxant treats spasticity from spinal cord injuries or MS and is sometimes used off-label for alcohol withdrawal — what is it?
Baclofen: Gabapentinoid and Skeletal Muscle Relaxant.

This steel-gray, brittle alkaline earth metal is found naturally only in combination with other elements, making up gemstones like aquamarine and emerald, and bonds so strongly to oxygen that extracting it is notoriously difficult — which element, atomic number 4?
Beryllium: Chemical element with atomic number 4 (Be)

Announced at the 1984 Farnborough Airshow and launched by Northwest Airlines, this advanced wide-body airliner added 6-foot winglets and a stretched upper deck to an already-famous jumbo jet design — which aircraft?
Boeing 747-400: Wide-body airliner, improved production series of the 747.

Branching from the windpipe at a landmark called the carina, these airway passages narrow progressively through several orders before losing cartilage support and changing name entirely — what are they called?
Bronchus: Airway in the respiratory tract.
Bearing distinctive fatty humps and used for milk, meat, and transport across deserts for millennia, which ungulate comes in a common one-humped form and a rarer two-humped form?
Its raw shell and seed are actually toxic until roasted or steamed, and the tropical American tree it grows on also yields a fleshy 'apple' — what is this familiar snack?
Cashew: Flowering plant in the family Anacardiaceae.
Also known as christophine or mirliton, this gourd-family fruit was first cultivated in Mesoamerica and is often cooked like summer squash — what is it?
Chayote: Edible fruiting vine of the gourd family.

An American naturalist who surveyed wildlife in Labrador, he turned his observations into quick-freezing methods that launched the modern frozen food industry — and a famous brand bears his name. Who was he?
Clarence Birdseye: American inventor, entrepreneur, and naturalist.

Though its wild populations are considered vulnerable to extinction, this domesticated freshwater fish has been introduced so widely that it's listed among the world's 100 worst invasive species — what is it?
Common carp: Species of fish. It gives its name to the carp family, Cyprinidae.
Spread mainly through the fecal-oral route, these single-stranded RNA enteroviruses share traits with poliovirus and rank among the leading causes of aseptic meningitis — which pathogens?
Coxsackievirus: Virus that causes digestive upset and sometimes heart damage.
This Harvard-trained legal scholar who wrote on criminal punishment and retribution joined Florida State's faculty in 2005, and was later murdered in a plot tied to his ex-wife's family — who is he?
Dan Markel: American law professor and murder victim (1972–2014)
This colorless, highly flammable liquid with a sweet smell was once widely used as a general anesthetic before modern alternatives — what compound?
After co-founding a social media giant, this entrepreneur left in 2008 to launch the workplace software company Asana — who is he?
Nicknamed the ALX, this Brazilian turboprop light-attack aircraft is assembled in Jacksonville, Florida with an American defense partner for low-threat counter-insurgency missions — which aircraft?
Embraer EMB 314 Super Tucano: Light ground attack and training aircraft.
Odorless, colorless, and dangerously sweet-tasting, this viscous compound goes into polyester fibers and antifreeze — and has even been spotted in outer space. What is it?
This principle describes how a changing magnetic field generates an electric current, underpinning the operation of transformers, generators, and motors — what is it called?
Faraday's law of induction: Basic law of electromagnetism.
Originally focused on water, this branch of physics studies liquids, gases, and plasmas, with applications from geophysics to aerospace engineering — which field?
Fluid mechanics: Branch of physics. Fluid mechanics is the branch of physics concerned with the mechanics of fluids (liquids, gases, and plasmas) and the forces on them.
Bound together by gravity, this vast system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter can range from a dwarf with under a thousand stars to a supergiant with a hundred trillion — what is it?
Galaxy: System of stars and interstellar matter. The word is derived from the Greek galaxias (γαλαξίας), meaning 'milky', a reference to the Milky Way galaxy that contains the Solar System.

Likely first domesticated by Austronesian peoples in Maritime Southeast Asia, this herbaceous perennial is grown for the spicy rhizome that puts it in the same family as turmeric and cardamom — what is it?
Ginger: Species of plant used as a spice.
Also known as the Congo variety, this African bird in the family Psittacidae lost its old 'African' nickname once a related Timneh species was split off as its own species — what is it?
Grown as deciduous shrubs across the temperate Northern Hemisphere and related to the birch family, this plant produces a popular round brown nut — which plant genus?
Discovered in 1910 and stored in mast cells and basophils, this compound triggers immune responses and doubles as a neurotransmitter in the brain, spinal cord, and uterus — what is it?
Histamine: Organic compound involved in immune responses.
Teaching philosophy and astronomy in Roman-era Alexandria, this Neoplatonist is considered the first female mathematician whose life is well documented — who is she?
Sitting on the electromagnetic spectrum between visible light and microwaves, this invisible radiation makes up most of the black-body glow given off by objects near room temperature — what is it?

Infrared: Form of electromagnetic radiation. Infrared (IR; sometimes called infrared light) is electromagnetic radiation (EMR) with wavelengths longer than that of visible light but shorter than microwaves.
Working under Tamerlane around 1400, this Persian astronomer and mathematician produced work that mostly never reached Europe and stays largely unpublished — who is it?
Jamshid al-Kashi: Persian astronomer and mathematician (c. 1380–1429)
Before flying on Space Shuttle mission STS-128 in 2009, this Mexican-American engineer helped develop digital mammography equipment at Lawrence Livermore — who is he?
José M. Hernández: American engineer, vintner, and former NASA astronaut.
Bred for their dazzling colors since the early 19th century in Niigata, Japan, these ornamental carp come in patterns like Kōhaku and Shōwa Sanshoku — what are they?
Koi: Colored varieties of Amur carp.

This small wild feline of South and Southeast Asia sports dark spots on a tawny coat and two stripes running from its eyes to its ears, and can live as high as 4,474 meters in the Himalayas — what is it?
Leopard cat: Small wild cat species. The leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis) is a small wild cat with dark spots on the tawny-coloured body and limbs.

Developed under the US Air Force's Advanced Tactical Fighter program, this American twin-engine stealth fighter was designed for air superiority but also handles ground attack, electronic warfare and signals intelligence — which aircraft?

Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor: American stealth air superiority fighter. The Lockheed Martin–Boeing F-22 Raptor is an American twin-engine, jet-powered, all-weather, supersonic stealth fighter aircraft.
Element number 12 is so eager to ignite that, once lit, it burns with a brilliant-white light — this lightweight alkaline-earth metal, less dense than aluminium, is what?
Magnesium: Chemical element with atomic number 12 (Mg)
Part of the chamomile tribe within the sunflower family, some species in this plant genus share the common name 'mayweed' — which genus?
Discovered in 1893 and existing as two mirror-image enantiomers, this CNS stimulant is best known in its hydrochloride-salt form nicknamed 'crystal' — what is it?

Also called 'selective sound sensitivity syndrome,' this disorder causes specific sounds to trigger strong negative emotional and physiological reactions, though it isn't yet listed in the DSM-5-TR — what is it called?
Misophonia: Disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds.
Native to the Americas from Texas down to Argentina, this domesticated waterfowl species has also gone feral in New Zealand, Australia, and parts of Europe — which species?
Muscovy duck: Species of bird. The Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) is a species of duck native to the Americas, from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas and Mexico south to Argentina and Uruguay.
A cable-like bundle of axons wrapped in three layers of connective tissue, this structure carries electrochemical signals called action potentials — what is it?
Nerve: Cable-like bundle of axons. The axons are bundled together into groups called fascicles, and each fascicle is wrapped in a layer of connective tissue called the perineurium.
Practitioners of this field are sometimes mistaken for mere coin collectors, but they study all means of paying debts — even the horses the Kyrgyz once used as currency. What's the field called?
Numismatics: Study of currencies, coins and paper money.
Described as far back as the 300s BC by Hippocrates, this bone infection most often strikes the spine in adults and the long bones in children — which condition?
Osteomyelitis: Infection of the bones. It may be acute or chronic and can be classified as hematogenous or non-hematogenous.

Native to southern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina, this vine produces a round berry that turns yellow or dark purple at maturity, prized for its juicy, seed-filled interior — what is it, scientifically speaking?
Passiflora edulis: Species of flowering plant in the passion flower family.
Named from a Tupi-Guarani word for tobacco filtered through French, this South American flowering plant genus is a garden hybrid favorite — which plant?
Petunia: Genus of flowering plants. The popular flower of the same name derived its epithet from the French, which took the word pétun, 'tobacco', from a Tupi–Guarani language.

Often stereotyped as ferocious predators, these South American freshwater fish actually have varied diets that include plant matter, making them more omnivorous than their reputation suggests. What fish are they?
Piranha: Common name for certain fishes of the family Serrasalmidae.
Chickens, turkeys, ducks, and geese all fall under this term for birds domesticated for meat, eggs, or feathers — what is it called?
Poultry: Domesticated birds kept by humans for their eggs, meat or feathers.
Forming the front-most part of the hip bone in vertebrates, this structure is made up of a superior ramus, an inferior ramus, and a body — which bone?
Pubis: Most forward-facing of the three main regions making up the os coxa.
Roughly 12 centimeters long in adults, this final section of the large intestine temporarily stores waste before it passes into the anal canal — what is it?
Rectum: Final portion of the large intestine. The rectum (pl.: rectums or recta) is the final straight portion of the large intestine in humans and some other mammals, and the gut in others.
Having spent years building theremins, this engineer debuted the first commercial synthesizer in 1964 and later the portable Minimoog — earning a spot in the Inventors Hall of Fame. Who is it?
Robert Moog: American electronic music pioneer (1934–2005)

The largest living reptile, whose males can top 1,000 kg and stretch six metres, ranges from India's coast through Southeast Asia to northern Australia — and earns its 'dangerous to humans' reputation. Which croc is it?
Saltwater crocodile: Species of reptile. It has been listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List since 1996.
As chief technology officer of a Turkish defense company, this pilot-engineer designed Turkey's first indigenous unmanned combat aerial vehicle and its first unmanned fighter jet. Who is he?
Selçuk Bayraktar: Turkish engineer and businessman. Selçuk Bayraktar (born 7 October 1979) is a Turkish pilot, engineer and businessman.
Housing the eyes, ears, nose, and brain, this bony structure at the head end of a vertebrate is built from cranial bones, facial bones, and tiny fused ossicles — what is it?
Skull: Bony structure that forms the head in vertebrates.
Sold under the brand name Aldactone, this diuretic medication treats heart failure and acne, and is also used to block testosterone's effects during feminizing hormone therapy — what is it?
NATO calls it 'Frogfoot' but its Soviet designers named it after the rook; this subsonic twin-engine jet first flew in 1975 to give close air support to ground forces — which aircraft?
Sukhoi Su-25: Soviet attack aircraft introduced 1978.
This Japanese immunologist shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with James P. Allison for identifying the PD-1 protein — who is he?
Tasuku Honjo: Japanese immunologist and Nobel laureate (born 1942)
With a half-life of roughly 14 billion years — about the age of the universe — the most stable isotope of this weakly radioactive metal decays into stable lead-208. Which element is it?
Thorium: Chemical element with atomic number 90 (Th)
Usually caused by a new genetic mutation rather than inherited, which disorder produces deformities of the ears, eyes, cheekbones, and chin but typically leaves intelligence normal?
Treacher Collins syndrome: Human genetic disorder. The degree to which a person is affected may vary from mild to severe.
A breakdown product of purine nucleotides found naturally in urine, elevated blood levels of this heterocyclic compound can trigger gout and kidney stones — what is it?
Uric acid: Organic compound. Uric acid is a heterocyclic compound of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen with the formula C5H4N4O3.
Named for the French word for 'watcher,' this paraphilia involves secretly observing strangers in private, intimate moments and gave rise to the nickname 'Peeping Tom' — what is it called?
Voyeurism: Sexual interest in or practice of spying on people engaged in intimate behaviors.

Ranging from microscopic to a record-breaking 58 meters long for one bootlace-shaped marine species, these limbless, usually eyeless invertebrates gave their name from the Old English 'wyrm' — what are they?
Which one below has the greatest length?
